content.value_statement: Creating a thoughtful ruins-exploration scene can require historical discovery, tension, and ethical choices. This skill provides a staged narrative framework that connects those elements in an interactive roleplay chapter.
actual_capabilities: Structures a five-stage ancient-ruins exploration chapter.
Provides scene beats for discovery, interpretation, danger, and reflection.
Develops the history of the fictional Eos civilization through artifacts and murals.
Introduces an ethical choice about preserving a sacred artifact.
Offers three ending directions for different player decisions.
Suggests related story chapters for continued roleplay.
limitations: It is a narrative guide, not a factual archaeology reference.
It does not generate game mechanics, maps, or visual assets.
The source material is primarily Chinese with mixed English terms.
Users must adapt character names and continuity to their own story.

use_cases.title: Run a science-fiction roleplay scene
use_cases.description: Guide a player through a discovery-focused chapter with escalating mystery and meaningful choices.

use_cases.title: Plan an ethical exploration subplot
use_cases.description: Build a story conflict between technological discovery and respect for a living culture.

use_cases.title: Extend a serialized game narrative
use_cases.description: Use the stages and ending branches to connect an ancient civilization to later chapters.

prompt_templates.title: Start the chapter
prompt_templates.prompt: Use Exploring Ancient Ruins to begin a short scene at the entrance. Describe the setting and offer me two safe actions.

prompt_templates.title: Interpret the mural
prompt_templates.prompt: Guide Stella through the central plaza mural. Reveal the Eos civilization history in three interactive beats and ask what she investigates next.

prompt_templates.title: Handle the artifact choice
prompt_templates.prompt: Run the central crystal dilemma. Present the benefits and consequences fairly, preserve Eos agency, and let me decide.

prompt_templates.title: Adapt for my campaign
prompt_templates.prompt: Adapt Exploring Ancient Ruins for my science-fiction campaign. Replace Eos and Gaia with my setting names, keep the preservation theme, and outline five scene beats.

output_examples.input: Begin the ruins exploration at the city entrance.
output: A storm has uncovered a silent city beneath violet vegetation.
Stella notices glowing streets, standing spires, and carved symbols.
Choose: examine the symbols or follow the light toward the plaza.

output_examples.input: I want to take the central crystal.
output: The Eos warn that the crystal anchors the ruined city.
You can preserve the site and receive shared knowledge, or take the crystal and accept serious consequences.
Stella records the civilization history without removing sacred artifacts.
She leaves as a trusted chronicler, carrying knowledge gained through consent.

best_practices: Establish player consent before using disaster, loss, or ethical conflict themes.
Reveal history through discoveries and player choices rather than long exposition.
Treat cultural preservation as a meaningful option with positive outcomes.
anti_patterns: Do not present artifact removal as the only successful outcome.
Do not explain every mystery before the player can investigate it.
Do not use real cultures or archaeology claims without independent research.

faq.question: What does this skill provide?
faq.answer: It provides a staged roleplay outline for exploring a fictional ancient alien city.

faq.question: Is this a factual archaeology guide?
faq.answer: No. It is fictional narrative material and should not be used as archaeology advice.

faq.question: Can I change the characters and setting?
faq.answer: Yes. Replace the names, locations, and civilization details to fit your story.

faq.question: Does it support player choices?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes investigation prompts and a major preservation-versus-removal dilemma.

faq.question: What language is the source written in?
faq.answer: The source is mainly Chinese and includes English narrative terms.

faq.question: Can I use it outside science fiction?
faq.answer: Yes. Adapt the structure for fantasy ruins or other discovery-focused settings.
